papers.title: Why We Created Yet Another Memory Framework: Understanding MGA's Role in Next-Gen Database Systems
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，带生产环境信号，关注延迟，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Despite the presence of multiple memory regions in modern database systems, supporting an efficient form of memory remains a challenge under production constraints. In enterprise-grade data systems, existing abstractions impose a trade-off between coarsegrained global sharing and strict process isolation, resulting in data copying, memory fragmentation, and limited support for controlled sharing. These challenges become more pronounced as workloads grow more diverse, and systems must tolerate process failures while maintaining predictable performance. This paper introduces the Managed Global Area (MGA), a scoped shared-memory abstraction in Oracle AI Database that addresses these limitations. MGA allows components to explicitly define allocation source, membership, and coordination semantics across selected processes while integrating with a production database engine. Unlike fully shared memory regions in Oracle, such as the System Global Area (SGA), MGA supports dynamic process membership and modular memory usage without imposing system-wide visibility. We evaluate MGA on analytical and AI workloads that stress shared-memory execution, including TPC-H hash joins and ONNX Runtime inference. Under concurrent execution, MGA reduces latency for join-intensive TPC-H queries by up to 35%. For ONNX-based inference, MGA-enabled model sharing reduces memory footprint by up to 90% and lowers large-model inference latency by up to 37%. These results demonstrate that dynamically scoped shared memory can improve both efficiency and predictability in production database systems.

papers.title: OceanBase Bacchus: A High-Performance and Scalable Cloud-Native Shared Storage Architecture for Multi-Cloud
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，带生产环境信号，涉及解耦式架构
papers.abstract: Although more databases embrace shared-storage architectures, current storage-disaggregated systems lack an optimal balance between cost and performance. B+-tree-based shared storage struggles with frequent in-place updates under high concurrency; disaggregated designs still require a scalable shared-log path for multi-writer OLTP. This paper presents OceanBase Bacchus, a production-grade disaggregated shared-storage architecture for OceanBase. We foreground two technical elements: (i) service-oriented PALF logging with sharded log streams and multiple Read-Write (RW) leaders, where partition-local ordering is composed with distributed 2PC across stream leaders, breaking the single-writer bottleneck of classic shared-log designs while preserving ACID, and (ii) a Shared Block Cache Service that pools macro-blocks within an availability zone, a less common alternative to purely per-node caches and motivated by stateless compute scaling. Cloud object storage backs the LSM-tree capacity tier for cost, but we do not treat "LSM + object storage" as the headline novelty (precedents exist). Bacchus's value is integrating and hardening these mechanisms in a shipping system, demonstrated by credible OLTP/OLAP performance and substantial storage-cost reductions. The architecture decouples modules and enables elastic scaling of compute, cache, and storage independently. Experimental results show that Ocean-Base Bacchus matches or exceeds HBase and PolarDB in OLTP and significantly outperforms StarRocks in OLAP. With multi-cloud support, the system retains high availability and competitive performance while cutting storage costs by 59% (OLTP) and 89% (OLAP).

papers.title: One Ring to Shuffle Them All: Scalable Intra-Process Data Redistribution with Ring-Buffer Shuffle in Redpanda Oxla

papers.abstract: As server CPUs scale to dozens and now hundreds of cores per socket, parallel query engines must rethink how they redistribute data between threads. Partitioned operators such as hash joins and aggregations require frequent data redistribution across threads, yet existing intra-process shuffle designs fundamentally fail to scale with core count: batch partitioning avoids cross-thread synchronization in the hot path but materializes all intermediate data, introduces a global producer/consumer barrier, and requires a consumption approach with low cache locality, while channel-based streaming avoids materialization but incurs per-channel synchronization that scales poorly with core count. As core counts rise, these architectural tradeoffs increasingly prevent engines from fully utilizing modern hardware. We present a ring-buffer streaming shuffle design that addresses these shortcomings through lock-free atomic slot acquisition into fixed-size batch groups, achieving amortized O (1) synchronization cost per batch and O (M) memory independent of input size. Ring-buffer shuffle has been implemented in Redpanda's Oxla query engine for two years, where it currently powers production queries for Redpanda SQL users. We evaluate all three approaches on a 72-core NVIDIA Grace-Hopper, a 192-core dual-socket AWS Graviton4, and a 96-core (192-thread) AMD EPYC. On a 72-core single-socket system the ring buffer outperforms channel streaming by up to 44% and batch partitioning by up to 79%; at 192 cores the advantage over channel grows to over 100% and over 300% versus batch partitioning. Even so, on chiplet architectures with many partitioned L3 caches, the shared atomic counter becomes a cross-die bottleneck and channel-based streaming remains competitive. End-to-end Graviton4 evaluation on TPC-H (21 queries) and ClickBench (43 queries) shows the advantage is workload-shape-dependent: the ring buffer wins TPC-H in aggregate (1.07×) across diverse query shapes, but a handful of consumer-heavy patterns—COUNT(DISTINCT), wide aggregates—favor channels and swing ClickBench's aggregate the other way.

To break this impasse, we propose ScaleSense, a proactive, query-level resource scaling framework. Specifically, it features a multi-faceted query encoder that jointly models plan topologies and hardware specifications. Crucially, a quantile-based resource predictor estimates multi-dimensional physical footprints, acting as a reliable safety net for optimal resource scaling. An auto-scaling controller then navigates the performance-cost Pareto frontier, dynamically tailoring allocations to specific business priorities without requiring model retraining. Evaluations on over 1.36 million production queries show that ScaleSense achieves state-of-the-art prediction accuracy with good prediction interval coverage. papers.title: E-LQO: A Comprehensive Energy Evaluation Framework for Learned Query Optimization
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，带基准测试，有实验评估，关注延迟
papers.abstract: Learned Query Optimization (LQO) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving database performance, with reported speedups of 2× to over 10× on standard benchmarks. Existing evaluations, however, remain largely latency-centric and leave the energy debt from data collection, model training, and online inference less visible. This paper presents E-LQO, the first comprehensive framework for evaluating energy consumption across the complete LQO lifecycle: data collection or preparation, model training, model inference, and plan execution. We formalize two domain-specific metrics— Energy Return on Investment (EROI) and Energy Payback Time (EPT)—to quantify both per-cycle efficiency and the amortization horizon of learned optimizers. Across seven LQO methods on fixed-scale JOB and on TPC-H/TPC-DS up to 100 GB, we find that lifecycle energy is governed less by whether an optimizer is learned than by how it obtains supervision. Execution-based systems buy plan quality through active exploration and carry a large upfront energy debt; passive/log-driven systems can repay much faster with reusable logs or labels, but this advantage depends on incremental-cost accounting and often comes with weaker latency gains on light workloads. We further show that total online inference energy, including candidate-plan generation, enables symmetric accounting, and that roughly 50% template coverage is the energy-optimal exploration region for the execution-based methods we study. E-LQO provides practitioners with actionable guidance for energy-conscious deployment decisions and exposes optimization opportunities for sustainable learned query optimization.

papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，有实验评估，关注延迟，涉及代价模型
papers.abstract: Modern cloud platforms provide diverse compute services, including virtual machines, Function-as-a-Service, and Query-as-a-Service, each offering unique trade-offs in performance, elasticity, and cost. While these services collectively cover the diverse needs of OLAP workloads, existing systems typically rely on a single service type or static rule-based scheduling. However, no single service is optimal for dynamic OLAP workloads with diverse performance characteristics and resource requirements. Consequently, efficient query execution requires scheduling workloads across heterogeneous services, which introduces three challenges. (1) Heterogeneous service models. Distinct billing models and execution paradigms (e.g., stateful or stateless) complicate the comparison of services. (2) Scheduling complexity at scale. High query concurrency exacerbates resource contention, creating a vast search space that makes identifying optimal scheduling decisions in real time computationally expensive. (3) Unpredictable runtime dynamics. Cloud infrastructure exhibits performance fluctuations due to factors like multi-tenant interference and scaling delays, which can invalidate initial scheduling decisions and cause suboptimal performance. In this paper, we present EASE, a resource-aware query scheduling framework designed to orchestrate OLAP queries across heterogeneous cloud compute services. EASE addresses these challenges through three integrated mechanisms. First, EASE incorporates a heterogeneity-aware cost model that captures distinct service characteristics to guide service selection. Second, EASE employs a real-time query scheduler that resolves resource contention under high concurrency. Third, EASE implements a dynamic rescheduler that mitigates runtime fluctuations by proactively migrating queries subject to unexpected delays. Our evaluation demonstrates that EASE significantly improves query performance and cost efficiency, reducing query latency by up to 35% and monetary cost by up to 67% compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

However, configuring HNSW remains challenging: its hyperparameters jointly affect search quality, latency, build time, and index size in nonlinear ways, while production deployments impose strict resource and tuning-time constraints. We study HNSW hyperparameter tuning from a systems perspective and show that its configuration space exhibits strong structural regularities. Specifically, we identify monotonic, dominant unimodal, and separable relationships among search-time and construction-time parameters, which induce feasibility boundaries under performance and resource constraints. Unlike generic black-box optimizers, CHAT exploits HNSW-specific structure to perform deterministic, sample-efficient search and prune resource-infeasible configurations before full index construction. An early prototype of GenDB uses LLM agents to generate instance-optimized query execution code tailored to specific data, workloads, and hardware resources. This prototype suits offline code generation for repetitive, templated queries, since the upfront generation cost amortizes over many executions and correctness can be ensured through extensive fuzz testing and manual inspection. For ad-hoc queries, GenDB can work with a traditional DBMS in a hybrid architecture: the DBMS handles one-off queries, while GenDB speeds up frequent SQL templates. We also discuss the current limitations of GenDB, such as high generation cost and the lack of correctness guarantees, to inform future extensions. A live demo is available at https://solidlao.github.io/GenDB/demo/.

Co-located architectures, which deploy both the row store and the column store on the same machine, degrade isolation due to shared resource contention. In this paper, we propose HeraDB, a GPU-accelerated HTAP database that achieves high-throughput transaction processing while maintaining strong performance isolation from analytical queries. To ensure query freshness, HeraDB introduces a hybrid CPU-GPU query execution strategy: the GPU path leverages massive parallelism to scan the stable but stale column-store snapshot, while the CPU path concurrently processes delta updates to retrieve complementary fresh results. To retrieve complementary results, HeraDB maintains timestamp-based filters on both paths. This design mitigates PCIe bottlenecks by synchronizing lightweight timestamp logs rather than massive delta updates. Evaluation on HATtrick shows that HeraDB outperforms Colibri in maximum individual TP/AP throughput, achieving up to 11.1× higher TP and 5.9× higher AP with high data freshness and strong performance isolation.

Existing systems fail to address these two concerns in a unified manner. Techniques that tightly control data staleness often constrain effective data skewness mitigation, while aggressive data skewness mitigation tends to exacerbate data staleness. As a result, systems are forced to trade off convergence for performance, or vice versa. To address this, we propose StaleFlow, an RL post-training system that jointly tackles data staleness and skewness. First, to control staleness, StaleFlow introduces a global consistency protocol that tracks the full lifecycle of each trajectory and constrains staleness. Second, to mitigate skewness, StaleFlow re-designs the RL system architecture by constructing data servers for trajectories and parameters to achieve flexible rollout coordination. We present NOMA as an integrated optimization loop in which plan generation, cost estimation, runtime refinement, and semantic caching reinforce one another across executions, setting a community-wide research agenda on query optimization for multi-agent systems.

papers.abstract: Many applications store records with structured columns and a text document, and ask how many records in a filtered set meet a criterion that only a reader of the text can judge, such as "How many patients with type 2 diabetes, aged 40 to 70, stopped metformin because their blood sugar stayed high?" An interactive application needs this count in seconds, as the user types the criterion, to decide whether the matching set is worth materializing with a batch pipeline in which an LLM judges the records. Prior approximate query processing over such semantic predicates has an expensive model, the oracle, label a sample at query time, so every query waits for the oracle. We present SignalCount, a production system that answers COUNT queries with structured and semantic predicates and calls no oracle at query time, even for ad-hoc criteria. Its oracle is the production LLM judge, and the judge's logged verdicts calibrate, offline, the fast classifier that already runs in front of the judge. At query time, SignalCount counts the filtered set exactly and draws a uniform sample of at most 1,000 records in one columnar scan, scores the sample with the classifier, and multiplies the average calibrated probability by the exact count. Its 90% interval combines a sampling term with one-sided, rate-dependent margins for calibration error, fitted by split conformal prediction across tenants. In a multi-tenant production deployment, latency has a p99 of 3.8 s and stays flat as the filtered set grows beyond the sample. On tenants held out from fitting, the interval covers the count that the production pipeline returns in 92% of estimates, although estimates run about 15% high in aggregate, because a calibration nearly unbiased per record is still biased per criterion.

papers.abstract: Intersecting sets of integers is a fundamental operation in search engines and graph analytics. Ranges absent from at least one operand are pruned without examining individual elements, fixed-width leaf segments map directly onto SIMD registers, and the structure extends naturally to k -way intersection via simultaneous descent. Morphing-node layouts adjust each node's size by occupancy, reducing memory usage by up to 8× on sparse data while minimally affecting throughput on dense data. We also evaluate PRISM on three real-world case studies: the Star Schema Benchmark, a TPC-H trigram index, and inverted list intersection on ClueWeb09. On all three, PRISM is the fastest method for intersection-heavy workloads, ahead of compressed-bitmap methods and more than an order of magnitude faster than general-purpose ordered and hash-based containers.

However, prior implementations of SPM primarily rely on background performance verification processes, delaying regression detection and recovery. This issue is amplified in autonomous cloud database systems, where several automatic actions that could cause plan change driven regressions are performed with limited customer control. Timely detection and remediation is paramount, but the constrained background resources on cloud may not keep pace. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Real-Time SPM in Oracle 26ai, a novel extension of SPM that performs foreground verification of new execution plans during user query execution. Real-Time SPM leverages runtime session context to immediately validate plan changes, enabling rapid adoption of superior plans while promptly detecting and preventing regressions. This paper presents the architecture and design of Real-Time SPM - including technical challenges like reliably comparing performance of previous plans - and contrasts it with traditional background plan evolution. Our experiments highlight tangible benefits of Real-Time SPM - delivering immediate performance boost while preserving plan stability in both cloud-native and on-premise environments. papers.abstract: Fast estimation of the size of the largest overlap between tables enables blocking and query-by-table retrieval in large table repositories. However, accurate estimation in heterogeneous repositories remains limited by three challenges: (C1) overlap depends on row-column structure, i.e., each matched cell must preserve both its row and column membership under a joint alignment of the two tables, but existing encodings leave this structure to be inferred indirectly; (C2) independent encoding provides no explicit channel for inter-table alignment signals, biasing prediction toward global similarity; (C3) naïve value encodings overfit to corpus-specific distributions, causing cross-domain degradation. Hence, we propose ALORE, a scalable and domain-robust overlap ratio estimator built on three principles: (P1) explicitly represent row-column structure; (P2) expose inter-table alignment signals during training without expensive alignment search; (P3) reduce sensitivity to corpus-specific value distributions. ALORE instantiates these principles with a Two-View Row-Column Hypergraph encoder, alignment-guided objectives with inexpensive interaction signals, and a domain-robust value mapping. Experiments on datasets spanning diverse domains and scales, including a large real-world corpus beyond prior benchmarks, show that ALORE outperforms the state of the art. ALORE reduces MAE by up to 55% overall and 69% in zero-shot transfer, while achieving up to 89x speedup. We further validate its effectiveness for query-by-table retrieval.

We first apply a core–tree decomposition to split the graph into a tree-like periphery and a dense core. The periphery is isolated via TreeIndex—a compact hierarchical tree labelling that exploits the nonzero pattern of the Cholesky factors of the inverse Laplacian. In the core, random walks mix rapidly and thus erase few cycles; we propose CoreIndex, which stores the DAG encoding the erased cycle structure over the core. This design yields near-linear index size and build time, and low query latency in practice on graphs with a core–periphery structure. Evaluating a new scheduler in a system is equally difficult, requiring time-consuming and costly experiments for many scenarios. To tackle this problem, we formalize the distributed task scheduling problem (DTS). Further, we present DQSim, a fine-grained simulator for distributed query execution that estimates the execution time of DTS schedules. This allows us to accurately model the effects of new scheduling algorithms without having to rebuild large parts of a system. DQSim can run thousands of experiments with user-defined system and cluster configurations and queries in seconds to evaluate scheduling techniques quickly. papers.title: Guixu: Valuation-Driven Data Discovery for Autonomous AI Agents with On-Chain Attestation
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents increasingly rely on external data to complete downstream tasks such as model training and decision support. However, existing data discovery systems remain largely retrieval-oriented: they surface candidate datasets from heterogeneous sources, but provide limited support for estimating task-specific utility, selecting cost-effective datasets under budget constraints, or incorporating trustworthy feedback from prior usage. This paper presents Guixu, a valuation-driven data discovery system for autonomous agents. Guixu employs a three-phase valuation pipeline with proxy-label propagation and multi-round knapsack optimization for task-aware data valuation. Guixu integrates agentic payment protocol to enable budget-constrained data procurement workflows. Guixu leverages on-chain data market and attestation signals for verifiable data discovery. Our demonstration highlights how Guixu enables an agent to move beyond keyword-based dataset retrieval toward task- and budget-aware, trustworthy data discovery and procurement. Attendees can interactively explore the full workflow, from NL task specification and multi-source search to data valuation and verifiable transaction feedback.

papers.title: Hermes at Scale: Powering Distributed Queries with a Unified Memory Fabric
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: MySQL is a widely used database management system. However, it has clear deficits for analytical workloads. To improve analytical performance, we introduced Hermes as an accelerator for MySQL. Since many workloads easily fit a single node/machine, we originally developed Hermes for this case. However, Hermes on a single node has a major limitation: Storage space is limited to a single-node, even worse, to main memory of a single node. In this paper, we address this problem by making Hermes distributed. New nodes can be added that bring additional resources, i.e. memory and compute, to the cluster. Hermes' storage can automatically expand to the new nodes. Our design operates as logically "Shared Memory" via an abstraction layer (Memcom). We argue that modern interconnects make shared memory feasible without extreme performance penalties. To further minimize sending data over the network, we annotate larger data blocks with localities, which allows reader nodes to locate and read local data. In addition, we extended Hermes' query execution to multiple nodes as well. This is implemented via a new Planner that splits the query plan into tasks and defines how query execution is parallelized (MPP intra-query parallelism). Each task is separated via data sharing operators (Portals) that write intermediates to a shared memory pool (Memcom). We extended scans to pick up row groups (our granularity of data storage) based on their locality. Therefore, distributed scans will preferably read local data (thanks to our predefined localities) and only when there is no more local data to be read consider remote data. We experimentally show that our approach is not only competitive in terms of performance but outperforms well-known open-source systems by more than 11×. Compared to industrial-grade cloud systems, Hermes also outperforms by 1.5×.

papers.title: No Silver Bullet: Boosting GaussDB Performance on the 30TB TPC-H Workload
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现
papers.abstract: GaussDB is Huawei's premier database system, designed for large-scale deployments and the most demanding workloads. It is a distributed shared-nothing system, capable of handling all types of workloads. This paper outlines a series of modifications to GaussDB aimed at improving its performance on large-scale and complex analytical workloads. After these changes, its performance on the TPC-H workload exceeded the best published result by 40% at 30 TB. The key enhancements to achieve this elite performance include adopting a pipeline execution model, a faster and more scalable inter-node data shuffle, exploiting a unified bus and unified remote memory access. We also expanded the support of cost-based Bloom filter placement and implemented several Bloom filter streaming strategies, enabling their use across nodes.

papers.title: Living Context Graphs: Continual Semantic Learning for Enterprise Data Reasoning
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，有实验评估，关注延迟
papers.abstract: Enterprise AI can now perform analytics, reporting, and data-driven workflows, yet the data foundations it relies on remain hard to operationalize: business meaning, relationships, metric definitions, and reporting conventions are absent from database schemas and scattered across undocumented systems and tribal knowledge. We introduce the Living Context Graph (LCG), a continually learned context layer that makes existing enterprise data operational for AI without requiring a copy or transformation of the underlying warehouse. LCG bootstraps base semantics and relationships from the data itself, builds a concept graph that indexes business context as queries are served, writes durable semantic learnings from verified outcomes, and withdraws or re-earns context when later outcomes contradict prior routes. We evaluate LCG through text-to-SQL, a core data-reasoning task, on a transfer-aware split of three BIRD databases comprising 499 questions: 353 form the learning history and 146 are held out and never used to update the context layer. Bootstrapping alone improves overall accuracy by +4.6 percentage points. Learning only from the history raises accuracy on the untouched held-out transfer set by +22.6 points (95% CI [+14.4, +30.8]), exceeding five-shot retrieval from the same history by +12.3 points. Incremental learning reaches the one-shot endpoint within observed evaluation noise on every database. Ablating the graph changes held-out accuracy by at most one question per database but increases per-query cost 2.3-3.3x and median latency 1.8-3.4x: continually learned semantics drive accuracy, while the graph makes that context efficient to serve.

papers.title: MoL-SQL: A Controlled Benchmark for Mixture-of-Language Text-to-SQL

papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems are usually built and evaluated under a monolingual assumption, yet in international applications users often query databases stored in a different language. Existing multilingual benchmarks mostly translate only the question without aligning schema and value entities, so they can neither locate the source of an accuracy drop nor rule out translation errors. Hence, we introduce MoL-SQL, a benchmark for mixture-of-language Text-to-SQL that switches the languages of the question, schema, and stored values independently while keeping each task fixed, and grades every cross-lingual entity mapping into four difficulty levels. We migrate five Text-to-SQL benchmarks of different domains and source languages through a unified alignment pipeline that builds a shared cross-lingual entity map, migrates each database with its constraints, rewrites the gold SQL under execution-equivalence checks, and regenerates the question from the verified SQL, keeping all language versions of a task aligned in entities, intent, and execution result. MoL-SQL provides two splits: MoL-Full (16,892 samples) for overall evaluation and MoL-Cube (3,840 samples) covering every language combination to isolate question, schema, and value effects. Experiments with eight LLMs and four families of Text-to-SQL methods show that schema and value languages have distinct effects, with stored values costing up to 23 points, and that these effects mainly stem from cross-lingual entity mapping. Neither question translation nor additional reasoning narrows the value gap, whereas access to target-database values substantially reduces it, indicating that mixture-of-language Text-to-SQL benefits most from language-aware context grounding.

papers.title: SIMQ: A Single Graph-based Index for Multi-Vector Query

papers.abstract: Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT achieve state-of-the-art effectiveness by representing documents as sets of token-level vectors and scoring via MaxSim, but their high computational cost limits scalability to large corpora. Existing approximate methods face fundamental bottlenecks: centroid interaction matrix approaches require computing a full matrix at every query and rely on GPU-accelerated clustering, while data-oblivious compression methods yield unstable recall that requires repeated compensation. We propose SIMQ (Single graph Index for Multi-vector Query), a framework that bridges single-vector graph indices and multi-vector retrieval through data-aware sampling-based clustering and per-token graph navigation, simultaneously bypassing all aforementioned bottlenecks. SIMQ organizes all token vectors into fine-grained clusters via data-aware sampling, builds a single graph index over cluster centroids independently of PLAID's residual representation, and approximates the MaxSim score through per-token graph search without materializing any interaction matrix or relying on GPU acceleration. We provide theoretical analysis showing that, under a manifold assumption and successful cell retrieval, data-aware partitioning has a smaller expected approximation error than a data-oblivious partition. Building on this foundation, SIMQ+ further introduces count-based scoring and a dynamic candidate set to improve robustness across varying query conditions. Experiments on five benchmarks compare recall, throughput, and construction time against several baselines, primarily on CPU; large-scale PLAID k-means centroids are built on a separate GPU machine. SIMQ has been integrated into VSAG, an Ant Group's open-source vector search library.

papers.title: Mind the Trap As LLMs Guess the Data Model: Grain-Aware Guards Against Fan-out in Text-to-SQL and Its Benchmarks
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，带基准测试，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Text-to-SQL systems built on large language models (LLMs) often aggregate over one-to-many and many-to-many joins, a classic trap: when the joined rows repeat an entity, a SUM or COUNT counts it more than once, yet the query runs and returns a plausible number. We characterize these fan-out errors by one condition on the relation an aggregate reads, which depends on two facts a schema does not show: each measure's grain, and how many rows a join on each key repeats. An audit that tests the condition on the data finds distorted gold answers for 4.2% of the dev questions of BIRD, a widely used benchmark, and BIRD's later, independent revision changed 44% of the answers the audit flags as definite fan-out, against 16% of unflagged ones. We release BIRD-FanOut, 486 BIRD questions with reviewed gold, and GrainTraps, synthetic questions that set this trap and related ones. Across eight LLM agents, functional dependencies (FDs) computed from the data help no more than per-column statistics on GrainTraps, but grain-aware FDs, which also state each measure's grain and the repetition per key, cut fan-out errors on BIRD from 18.4% of runs to about 13%, also on held-out questions and without LLM judges. Accuracy rises less, because most remaining errors are not fan-out and BIRD's hints often prescribe the over-count. Text-to-SQL models should be given the grain of the data, and benchmark gold should be audited on the data. Code, data and benchmarks are available at https://github.com/ahmed-mahran/misqal

papers.title: SJG: A Skyline Joint Graph for Multi-Component Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
papers.importance_reason: 贴近真实场景，关注吞吐，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Graph-based indexes enable efficient approximate nearest neighbor search at scale by linking similar objects. In applications such as product retrieval and rental listing search, similarity depends on several components whose relative importance varies across queries. The challenge is that the index must select neighbors during construction, but the query weights that determine which objects are closest are not yet known. A straightforward approach is to index each component separately. However, merging the results of these searches can miss the nearest neighbor under the weighted distance. A joint graph allows a search to follow links across components, helping to avoid such misses, but selecting neighbors separately within each component can leave redundant edges, and keeping component hierarchies synchronized limits parallel construction. To address these limitations, we propose the Skyline Joint Graph (SJG). Although query weights can change the ranking of candidate neighbors, the dominance relation among them is independent of those weights. SJG exploits this property by pooling candidates across components and retaining the Skyline for each node, thereby enabling efficient approximate nearest neighbor search under different query weights while supporting parallel graph construction. Extensive experiments on six real-world datasets demonstrate that SJG achieves up to $27.9\times$ the query throughput of baseline methods at 90% Recall@10, while accelerating single-threaded index construction by up to $201\times$. Its index requires at least 36% less space than the smallest baseline index.

papers.title: G-CasDec: General Cascaded Decompression on GPUs
papers.importance_reason: 涉及压缩
papers.abstract: GPU-accelerated analytical query processing is often limited by both GPU device memory capacity and host-to-device data transfer time. Modern data compression techniques, such as cascaded lightweight compression, can mitigate these issues. However, existing designs all exhibit critical tradeoffs on compression ratios, decompression speed, and extensibility. They either apply aggressive compression without addressing execution irregularity, or maintain strictly aligned data layouts that sacrifice compressibility. Also, none of them provides an extensible way to easily add new schemes. To address these issues, we present G-CasDec, an optimized framework to enable efficient decompression on GPUs for general cascaded compression schemes. G-CasDec incorporates several key techniques, including aligned batching for aggressive compression of variable-length data yet with efficient decompression, shared memory reuse and register-level fusion to improve resource utilization, and a set of bytecode instructions to orchestrate a generic decompression flow. G-CasDec outperforms state-of-the-art designs with 2.8× higher compression ratios and 2.0× faster decompression, and is also extensible to arbitrary cascade schemes.

papers.title: HyperDBDiag: Multi-Root-Cause Identification and Operator-Level Localization for Database Performance Anomalies
papers.importance_reason: 带生产环境信号，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Database performance anomalies in modern production environments are not always triggered by a single cause. Instead, they often arise from the concurrent interaction of multiple causes within the same time window, posing substantial challenges to accurate operator-level root-cause analysis. When multiple root causes interact through shared resources, metric anomalies may be amplified, attenuated, or masked. Consequently, salient local anomalies may no longer correspond directly to the actual root causes, making conventional single-path diagnosis and shallow correlation-based methods prone to misdiagnosis. To address this challenge, we propose HyperDBDiag, a method for multi-root-cause identification and operator-level localization of database performance anomalies. HyperDBDiag connects root causes, performance metrics, SQL templates, and execution operators in a knowledge graph, captures joint anomaly patterns across metrics with a metric hypergraph, and uses a constrained LLM to determine the final root-cause set and provide remediation suggestions. When finer-grained localization is possible, HyperDBDiag also identifies the associated anomalous SQL statements and execution operators. We evaluate HyperDBDiag on a database performance anomaly dataset constructed using DB-MAGS. Experimental results show that HyperDBDiag effectively reduces graph complexity while improving root-cause localization accuracy.

papers.title: Decision Columns as an Index: Interpretable Embeddings for Explainable Entity Matching and Search

papers.abstract: Business data systems must determine whether records refer to the same entity and retrieve records satisfying requests whose decisive properties are implicit. As agents act on these records, both tasks require auditable reasons. Dense embeddings perform well but offer opaque coordinates, cannot be filtered by meaning, and require corpus re-encoding to add new properties. We propose interpretable embeddings built from decision columns: each column stores a decision model's calibrated answer to a natural-language question, with outcomes yes, no, or not stated. A record's embedding is its answers across an ordered set of questions. Similarity decomposes exactly into per-question contributions, and new questions add coordinates without altering existing ones. On public product benchmarks, question-space retrieval matches dense candidate generation statistically in a retrieve-then-verify entity matcher, while providing exact explanations for accepted matches. Questions derived from retrieval failures triple mean reciprocal rank without re-encoding prior answers. For search, inferring the attributes of a suitable result outperforms encoding only the literal request, and combining question-space and dense scores improves retrieval, though not at our prespecified confidence threshold. A single small neural network predicts the full interpretable vector from an existing dense embedding, enabling corpus backfilling from a few thousand labeled rows at roughly 1/200 the cost. We position interpretable embeddings as a complementary, readable retrieval channel for explaining matches, filtering on attributes, and extending indexes as failures expose missing facts.

papers.title: Cache Replacement in Direct-Access Cloud OLAP-An Experimental Comparison and Practical Guidance
papers.importance_reason: 有系统实现，关注延迟
papers.abstract: Direct-access cloud OLAP engines rely on local caches to hide remote object-store latency, yet the replacement design space remains poorly understood. Existing systems largely inherit recency- or Clock-oriented policies from DBMS buffer management, even though cloud misses combine a size-independent request overhead with a size-dependent transfer cost and cache objects vary widely in size. We present a broad experimental comparison of 22 cache-replacement algorithms and one semantic-caching baseline across seven analytical workloads and ten cache sizes. To compare them on a common basis, we formulate Unified Hit Ratio (UHR), a latency-weighted hit ratio that decomposes into a workload-specific weighted combination of object and byte hit ratios, and equivalently, the normalized fraction of aggregate remote-download latency saved by caching. Our results yield practitioner-oriented guidance. Classical size-aware policies developed outside the DBMS literature remain surprisingly strong, dominating object hit ratio on most workloads and staying near the UHR frontier. Byte efficiency depends primarily on aggressive filtering of zero-reuse objects, while under multi-tenant drift lightweight per-request adaptation is often more robust than retraining-heavy learned methods. We instantiate these lessons in LARA, a compact reference policy that validates the guidance through competitive UHR performance.

papers.title: Data Agents Need a Map: Evolving, Demand-Driven Knowledge of Large Collections

papers.abstract: Most data that could power rich analysis sits unintegrated and uncataloged in open data portals, data lakes, and collections of independently published tables. Data agents now answer analytical questions over such collections with a full workflow per question, including dataset retrieval, join discovery and evaluation, and tailored program synthesis, most of which are discarded when a new task arrives. The knowledge these workflows depend on, such as what each column means, which context a dataset leaves implicit, and how datasets combine, is therefore perpetually rederived and never persisted. We argue for persisting this knowledge in an evolving semantic atlas that users and agents can navigate and extend. The atlas describes every dataset offline, through topics, semantic types, and profiles, so that agents can find the datasets that a task requires. Relationships between datasets and integrated views, which require comparing datasets, are instead built on demand for the areas of analysis that users declare. Every item is stored with its provenance and the confidence of the methods that produced it, so that agents can decide how far to trust it or whether to abstain. As datasets change, inconsistencies are detected and corrected automatically, while human users settle what the data leaves inconclusive. We present this vision and its challenges, namely building the atlas over large, multi-domain collections, keeping it correct and up to date, serving it to users and agents, and evaluating whether it improves their answers. A proof of concept on DAB, a benchmark for data agents, shows that with only part of the atlas a coding agent can already read a fifth to a third fewer tokens while achieving the same accuracy as without it.

papers.title: KaleidoKV: Rearranging Evidence for Efficient KV Cache Reuse in Offline RAG Inference
papers.importance_reason: 关注吞吐，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) augments large language models (LLMs) on question-answering (QA) tasks with retrieved evidence at inference time. Related questions in an offline batch often retrieve overlapping evidence, but prefix caching reuses key-value (KV) states only for identical token prefixes, making reuse dependent on evidence order. Although all questions and evidence are known before execution, existing reordering methods commit to early grouping decisions and can miss sharing opportunities that require several requests to move together. Evaluating alternative layouts can incur planning costs that offset inference savings, while concurrent requests may still recompute shared prefixes before their KV states become available. To address these challenges, we propose KaleidoKV, a framework that plans evidence orders across the batch and controls when requests enter the engine while preserving each request's evidence set and content. Joint layout planning revises formed groups through coordinated request moves and keeps a move only if it lowers planned prefill, the computation required when each shared prefix is computed once. A global prefix index selects evidence orders by locating reusable prefixes and evaluates each move incrementally from only the affected request paths. Prefix-ready admission tracks nested prefix dependencies, delaying requests whose shared prefixes are still being computed while allowing independent requests to proceed. Experiments on four QA workloads and four LLMs show that KaleidoKV achieves the highest throughput and lowest mean time to first token in all 16 settings, with approximately 1.24-1.75x the throughput of the strongest baseline, including planning time. With Llama-3.1-8B under the default configuration, actual prefill stays within 0.5% of planned prefill across all four workloads.

papers.title: Shoonya: Zero-Socket In-Process Small Language Models for Graph Databases with Schema-Epoch KV Caching, Live Catalog Logit Masking, and Verifier-Advantage Distillation

papers.abstract: Coupling a property-graph database to an external language-model server imposes a three-part socket tax: serialization overhead dwarfing microsecond graph reads, repeated prefill of verbose schemas, and blind decoding divorced from the live catalog and multi-version concurrency control (MVCC) engine. Direct GraphStore references unlock three database-native primitives: (1) an epoch-invalidated SchemaPrefixCache over a copy-on-write PagedKvArena accelerating warm CPU time-to-first-token by 4.91x--13.68x with O(1) DDL invalidation; (2) a 36 us columnar catalog and source-span logit mask enforcing valid ontology identifiers and verbatim spans; and (3) a sub-65 us read-only MVCC gate serving Tier-0 queries inside 389.8 MiB INT8 RSS (59.8--67.9 tok/s) with 0.0% hallucination leak. Rank-factorized tied embeddings (-74.5% vocabulary weights), atomic indentation tokens (0/421 indentation errors), 4:1 grouped-query attention with 2:1 cross-layer KV sharing (-93.75% INT8 KV memory), Warmup-Stable-Decay training, KnOTS SVD merging, Step-GRPO, and Rust Jacobi SVD governance keep 100% of layers heavy-tailed ($α\in [1.88, 2.20]$). Finally, we synthesize nine lessons across v0.1--v1.0, resolving a Reverse-Token-Density Distillation Trap via teacher scaling and zero-VRAM Verifier-Advantage-Gated Knowledge Distillation (AdvKD), recovering +13.61 MBPP points (33.07%) while reaching 100% validity on enrichment, grounded extraction, and tool planning.

papers.title: Agent Recovery Gone Wrong: Measuring Harm Beyond Duplicate Calls

papers.abstract: Code-executing LLM agents submit blocks of code that issue several API writes. If a block fails after some of its writes have taken effect, the agent rewrites the block and continues. It is unknown how often such a recovery harms the external state when the failure occurs naturally in the code written by the agent. In this paper, we measure it on recorded trajectories of AppWorld agents. In a stratified random sample of 200 candidate episodes across ten models, 145 are partial executions confirmed by the database state. In the sample, 30 of 143 confirmed partial executions with a determinable outcome are followed by a harmful recovery, and its violation remains at the end of the run, which gives a stratification-weighted estimate of 24.6%. Two thirds of the harmful recoveries duplicate an effect, and the rest delete user data or make a wrong first-time write, e.g., an order of a wrong product. A rule that searches for repeated calls finds 75% of duplications but only 41% of all harm. We also examine two sources of operation identity for an idempotency contract. In a small pilot (17 episodes, one local model), identifiers supplied by the model do not detectably reduce harm, because the model issues a new identifier for the same operation. Identity derived from the call content, evaluated counterfactually on the sample, would have matched every harmful write in 14 to 18 of the 30 harmful recoveries, but in none of those with a wrong first-time write, and it would also have matched writes required by the task in 30 episodes. Based on these results, we outline design requirements for safer agent recovery.

papers.title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?

papers.abstract: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. papers.title: STORMGUIDE-FL: Stochastic Remote Guidance for Efficient Mining of Federated Streaming Data

Existing solutions still face two major challenges: local concept drift, where each client's data distribution shifts over time, and global client drift, arising from asynchronous engagement and imbalanced contributions across heterogeneous training participants, formally described as dual client heterogeneity. We propose STORMGUIDE-FL, a federated optimization and data-mining framework that mitigates both types of drift using a server-guided pipeline for data acquisition and local training. For data acquisition, a lightweight client-side sampling strategy incrementally selects informative and diverse instances from non-stationary, non-IID local streams under bounded memory, compute, and labeling budget. For local training, the server's remote guidance is embedded directly into local optimization as an update-level correction, counteracting client drift without discarding scarce labeled samples. We empirically verify the effectiveness of the proposed sampling strategy on federated data streams across gradual, sudden, and recurring concept drift, and demonstrate that its gains compound with the update-level drift correction. Experimental results further show improved speed and robustness of global model convergence under resource-constrained, heterogeneous conditions.

papers.title: Tight Width Minimisation of Self-Join-Free Quantified Conjunctive Queries

papers.abstract: Query minimisation is a classical problem in database theory and the width of a formula, defined as the maximum number of free variables over all subformulae, is a central measure for query evaluation. We study width minimisation for a subclass of quantified conjunctive queries (QCQs), namely self-join-free QCQs. For this subclass, we show that rewriting optimality coincides with semantic optimality: given a query $φ$, the minimum-width query obtainable from $φ$ by applying natural and established rewriting rules has minimum width among all first-order formulae logically equivalent to $φ$. As a consequence, the width of a self-join-free QCQ can be optimised by a logical-equivalence-preserving rewriting algorithm.

papers.title: Logical Design Tuning via Workload-aware E/R-to-Relational Mapping

papers.abstract: Conceptual data models, like the E/R model, can provide a more stable and intuitive user-facing interface and better logical independence for applications, compared to the relational model which is forced to closely mirror the physical representation. However, this flexibility introduces a challenge as well as an opportunity: a single conceptual schema admits many semantically equivalent relational schemas, whose performance can differ substantially across workloads. Traditional mapping methods use a set of predefined transformation rules or designer-selected mapping strategies, rather than optimizing the relational realization with respect to the expected workload. In this paper, we present a cost-based framework for workload-aware conceptual-to-relational mapping. Given an E/R schema and a representative workload, our framework automatically selects an efficient relational schema by optimizing mapping decisions, including inheritance, entity and relationship representations. User-specified E/R queries are compiled into SQL over the selected relational realization, allowing existing relational query optimizers to determine the physical execution plan. Experiments on real-world-inspired schemas show that mapping choices strongly affect performance; fixed or heuristic strategies exhibit large variability across workloads, whereas our approach consistently achieves competitive performance avoiding pathological cases.

papers.title: Towards Online Adaptive LLM-based Semantic Filtering

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) enable semantic filtering over unstructured documents using natural language predicates, but invoking an oracle LLM on every document incurs prohibitive monetary cost and online latency. Existing model-cascade approaches reduce this cost by using a lightweight proxy model to score each document and forwarding only uncertain documents to the oracle. However, their proxy models have limited generalization capability, and they typically adopt fixed sampling budgets for proxy training and threshold calibration, which insufficiently adapts to diverse online queries. To address this, we present OASIS, an online adaptive framework for LLM-based semantic filtering. OASIS combines a query-agnostic document similarity prior with query-adaptive online learning and sampling. In the offline phase, OASIS utilizes query-agnostic document similarity as a prior and constructs a document navigating spread-out graph (NSG) over document embeddings. For each online query, OASIS trains a query-conditioned graph attention network over the document NSG to obtain proxy scores through semi-supervised node classification. To allocate labels effectively, OASIS adopts density-aware active learning to explore uncertain score regions, selectively annotate informative documents, retrain the proxy, and stop early when additional labels are unlikely to improve the cascade. During threshold calibration, OASIS progressively samples an adaptively sized calibration set, adapting calibration cost to the query's score distribution. Extensive experiments demonstrate that OASIS achieves a 1.75x-5.42x reduction in online latency and reduces the number of LLM-processed documents by 35%-75% relative to the state-of-the-art methods at an achieved accuracy of 0.9.

papers.title: Federated KPI Aggregation with Local Privacy Constraints and Coordinated OLAP Roll-Ups

papers.abstract: Cross-organizational KPI analysis can require aggregated results from independently administered data warehouses without centralizing detailed records. To limit disclosure from small local groups, a site can require a minimum number of contributing records before releasing a KPI value for a group. If each site applies this rule independently, different local contributions may be suppressed and the combined KPI can become incomplete. This paper investigates whether OLAP granularity can be coordinated before local query results are released so that all sites satisfy their local minimum-cohort rules and contribute at the same analytical level. The proposed method selects the least-generalized common roll-up accepted by every site. Site agents coordinate current capabilities and approved local execution across independently administered sites, with privacy checks and aggregate computation remaining deterministic local functions. In a four-site prototype, coordinated roll-up retained all contributions and reproduced the corresponding centralized result, compared with 78.3% retained under independent suppression. A capability-change experiment showed fewer candidate checks and replies and no unsupported requests when current site-agent state was used. The results demonstrate the feasibility of federated KPI aggregation under local privacy constraints through coordinated granularity selection and agent-based coordination.

papers.title: GenSPARQL: A Generative Extension of SPARQL for Incomplete Knowledge Graphs
papers.importance_reason: 有实验评估，涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Knowledge graphs on the Web are incomplete, and SPARQL answers a query only from the stored triples. Large language models (LLMs) can predict missing facts, but an LLM returns names instead of IRIs and requires one call per binding of a query variable. We present GenSPARQL, a generative extension of SPARQL 1.1 with an operator GENOP that binds values generated by an LLM to query variables during query evaluation. A similarity join maps generated names to entities of the graph, and the query planner invokes the LLM only for the bindings selected by the other graph patterns and filters. In a web workbench, attendees query two graphs built from Wikidata and inspect generated values, mapped entities and LLM calls. In our evaluation with three open-weight LLMs, the embedding similarity maps 83% of the entities named by the LLMs and yields only one incorrect match.

papers.title: Provably Near-Optimal PQ in the Extended Zador Model
papers.importance_reason: 涉及代价模型
papers.abstract: This paper investigates Product Quantization (PQ) Optimization with Gaussian data. It offers three key contributions (i) a proof that SVD is the optimal preconditioning rotation for PQ; (ii) a new Extended Zador (EZ) estimator of the $k$-means quantization cost that is accurate in low bit rates and low dimensions; and (iii) a novel segmentation algorithm based on 1-d bin packing of global bit allocations. The result is a simple algorithm (EZPQ) with strong approximation guarantees. It matches OPQ's empirical accuracy while providing a per-instance distortion lower bound certificate under the Gaussian EZ cost model. On typical real embedding spectra, EZPQ with 2 bits per coordinate is often certifiably within 1% of the optimum in this model. It also consistently achieves a lower reconstruction error than all random-rotation-based algorithms such as EDEN, E-RaBitQ, and TurboQuant.

papers.title: Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal for Schema Retrieval in Text-to-SQL
papers.importance_reason: 涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: LLM-based natural-language interfaces to relational databases are gated by a schema-retrieval step: the generator can only be as good as the slice of schema it is shown. On a database with hundreds of tables, that slice must be selected and the selection is two-sided---omit a needed table and the query becomes unrecoverable, include too many and the irrelevant ones act as noise that degrades the model's output. When an agentic retriever that lets the model inspect the schema can be too costly or too slow, the fallback is an embedder that ranks tables by cosine similarity and keeps a top-k. This fallback has two weaknesses: a fixed budget is suboptimal question by question, and embedding similarity overlooks foreign-key-linked tables that are necessary for joins. We present Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal (AEGT, ElbowHop for short), a property-graph table retriever that addresses both: an adaptive elbow cutoff replaces the fixed budget with a per-question one under a single aggressiveness parameter, and bidirectional foreign-key traversal deterministically recovers the bridge tables embedding similarity misses. We evaluate the retriever on 3 corpora of increasing candidate-pool size (BIRD Mini-Dev queried per database, 3--13 tables; its eleven schemas merged, 74; and a merged Spider-train graph, 546) and isolate the two mechanisms under a per-question budget-matched protocol. Across these settings the adaptive elbow emerges as the dominant mechanism---at matched recall it roughly doubles precision over a fixed budget on the larger pools, the margin widening as the pool grows---while the foreign-key traversal pays off on the join-critical bridge tables dense retrieval cannot reach, in the single-hop tight-budget case. We characterize the method as a low-cost, recall-robust first stage for schema retrieval on which a downstream selection or generation step can build.

papers.title: Optimizing Query Decomposition for Reliable Validation
papers.importance_reason: 涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have made querying databases more accessible, but cannot guarantee that the SQL they generate is correct. Without a trusted reference query, a validator (human or LLM) must decide whether a generated query answers the intended question. Enterprise questions often require queries with multiple joins, nested subqueries, and multi-level aggregation, and validating such a query in one judgment is error-prone. Decomposition simplifies this task by rewriting a query into smaller queries (blocks) that recompose to the original, each checked against its own sub-question. Decompositions differ, however: smaller blocks make each judgment easier but require more judgments, and the best balance depends on the validator's ability. We formulate validation-aware query decomposition as an optimization problem. Just as a query optimizer chooses among equivalent plans by estimated cost, we choose among decompositions by how reliably a given validator is expected to check them. We model how task difficulty and validator ability jointly affect reliability and define an objective that balances reliability against the number of judgments. Over a space of decompositions derived from logical-plan rewrites, our search finds an optimal one. We implement it in DecoVal, a pipeline that presents each block with its sub-question and input interface, combines local verdicts into a query-level decision, and localizes errors to blocks. A user study shows that decomposition helps human validators catch and locate errors: with DecoVal, participants caught 91% of the errors, up from 36% without decomposition, and located the error in nearly every rejection. Experiments on BEAVER and Spider 2.0 with LLM validators show that DecoVal also raises error-detection recall over whole-query validation while keeping precision high, and that the best granularity depends on the validator.

papers.title: Growing Clusters Lower the Bar: Profile Accretion in LLM-Based Incremental Entity Resolution
papers.importance_reason: 涉及连接处理
papers.abstract: Incremental entity resolution pipelines ask a large language model (LLM) whether a new record belongs to an existing cluster and show it the records already linked. Analyses of matching oracles assume that the answer depends only on the records compared. For the LLM matchers we test, it depends on cluster size, and the model lowers its bar for joining a cluster as the cluster grows. On French procurement suppliers from FOPPA, with SIREN identifiers as ground truth, we hold the new record fixed and vary only the number of verified members shown. Sixteen members instead of one raise the false match rate on similarly named companies by \dfmrMin--\dfmrMax{} percentage points in six open-weight models, while their area under the ROC curve rises by only \aucGainMin--\aucGainMax. In Claude Sonnet~5 and Haiku~5.5 the rise is \clSonD{} and \clHaiD{} points. The shift persists with street addresses, prompt variants and the BatchER and ComEM formats, and one false merge raises acceptance of the intruder's other records in every open model. It does not arise on Czech and Bulgarian TED notices, where one record with its full address already identifies the company. In online linking on confusable blocks, a single threshold set on labelled data raises recall by a factor of \fxRRmin--\fxRRmax{} for five models with no detectable loss of precision and no extra LLM calls.

papers.title: A Design Space for Data Agents: Insights from KDD Cup 2026
papers.importance_reason: 有实验评估
papers.abstract: Data agents interpret analytical requests, gather evidence from heterogeneous sources, and compute results within finite resource budgets. We analyze the final code submissions of the ten highest-ranked teams in the KDD Cup 2026 Data Agents for Complex Data Analysis competition. We organize the observed design choices into three interacting layers, covering workflow orchestration, analytical functions, and working state. The comparison reveals recurring patterns for allocating computation in response to task progress, structuring evidence for computation and assessment, and preserving reusable artifacts with their provenance. Candidates that rely on the same evidence can inherit the same error, so interpreting their agreement requires tracing those dependencies. The design space motivates controlled evaluations of how resource allocation, evidence sharing, and targeted recovery affect task completion and correctness.

papers.title: Toward a Scalable and Adaptive Evaluation Measure for Time Series Anomaly Detection
papers.importance_reason: 有实验评估
papers.abstract: Time Series Anomaly Detection (TSAD) is a fundamental task for time series analytics. Unlike other domains, where anomaly detection mainly focuses on point-based anomalies, TSAD must also handle range-based anomalies. Nevertheless, TSAD methods are commonly evaluated with measures inherited from classification, such as Precision and Recall, which require a threshold, or with threshold-independent ones, such as AUC, which ignore the temporal aspect of anomalies. To address these issues, the Volume Under the Surface (VUS) measure scores detectors across all thresholds and a range of buffer lengths and has been widely adopted. However, VUS has two limitations. First, VUS is computationally expensive, requiring 7 hours and 38 minutes to evaluate 32 detectors on the 870 TSB-AD time series. Second, VUS applies the same buffer lengths to every anomaly and detector, which can yield over-optimistic scores that hinder discrimination between accurate and mediocre detectors. We first introduce FastVUS, which computes VUS exactly and on average 76x faster by (i) computing all buffers in parallel, (ii) pruning irrelevant buffers for the existence reward, (iii) casting the confusion matrix as a single reduced matrix multiplication, (iv) computing VUS for every buffer length in one pass, and (v) discarding non-anomalous regions with a global mask. We also develop FastVUS-GPU, which recasts every step as batched tensor operations and reaches an average 304x speedup with a maximum error of $5\times10^{-3}$. Building on FastVUS, we introduce AutoVUS, an adaptive extension that compares each detection against a random baseline and selects the buffer length that maximizes the gain over it. Our case studies show that AutoVUS reduces over-optimistic scores and better separates accurate from mediocre detectors. We release FastVUS and AutoVUS as open source to promote time-aware evaluation at scale.

papers.title: Read Boundaries in Agent Memory: Consistency, Completeness, and Repair
papers.importance_reason: 主题高度相关
papers.abstract: Agent-memory services assemble evidence through several reads across connections or stores. An update between those reads can pair an assertion with source content from another revision. We protect the complete recall, including enrichment and materialization, and evaluate the resulting evidence and service behavior in Hindsight and Cognee. A 600-run Cognee study compares unprotected recall, a repeated recall, a read/write lock, and optimistic epoch validation under default incremental updates and full rebuilds. At approximately 20 recalls/s, unprotected default updates yield 199 conflicting responses among 12,010 scheduled recalls with spaced writes and 284 among 12,010 with bursts. The lock and epoch validation each deliver complete, compatible evidence for all 24,020 default-update recalls. With default bursts, epoch validation reduces update p95 by 109 ms while adding 290 ms to recall p95 relative to the lock. A separate 160-run incremental-failure study distinguishes mixed revisions from complete new derived content whose canonical source record remains old. Both protected policies refuse service after failure; the first default retry restores all 80 fault runs through native full-rebuild fallback. In Hindsight, a shared PostgreSQL snapshot removes the mismatch in ten controlled pairs, with recall p95 rising from 19 ms to 29 ms. These results identify the read boundary needed for coherent evidence and the publication and recovery conditions governing service after an update fails.

papers.title: Compiling Existential-Positive Queries to Bounded-Variable Fragments
papers.importance_reason: 主题高度相关
papers.abstract: A crucial property of bounded-variable fragments of first-order logic is that they can be evaluated in polynomial time. It is therefore a useful preprocessing step to rewrite, if possible, a first-order query to a logically equivalent one with a minimum number of variables. However, it may occur that reducing the number of variables causes an increase in formula size. We investigate this trade-off for the existential-positive fragment of first-order queries, where variable minimisation is decidable in general. In particular, we study the blow-up in the formula size when compiling existential-positive queries to the bounded variable fragment of positive first-order logic. While the increase of the formula size is always at most exponential, we identify situations (based on the signature and the number of variables) where only a polynomial blow-up is needed. In all other cases, we show that an exponential lower bound on the formula size of the compiled formula that matches the general upper bound. This exponential lower bound is unconditional, and is the first unconditional lower bound for formula size with respect to the studied compilation; it is proved via establishing a novel interface with circuit complexity which may be of future interest.

papers.title: SYCLDB: A Cross-Vendor Heterogeneous Analytical DBMS
papers.importance_reason: 主题高度相关
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of AI and analytical workloads has increased the need for fast, interactive analytical data processing. This, in turn, has led to a surge of interest in designing accelerated analytical database engines that can exploit modern GPUs to scale computation. While GPUs provide the massive data-parallelism required by modern analytics, the software landscape remains dominated by closed-source, vendor-locked programming models, like CUDA, limiting portability across multi-vendor GPUs. In this work, we present SYCLDB, an end-to-end analytical database engine built upon the SYCL open standard, designed to enable efficient, hardware-agnostic execution across a wide range of accelerators using a single codebase. By implementing core relational operators as modular SYCL kernels, integrating them with a SQL frontend based on Apache Calcite and Apache Thrift, and supporting Apache Arrow for efficient columnar ingestion, SYCLDB reduces dependence on vendor-specific GPU programming stacks by enabling a single SYCL codebase to execute analytical query pipelines across Intel, AMD, and NVIDIA GPUs.
